items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the ratio of annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration (P ÷ PET); below 0.05 is hyper-arid, 0.05-0.20 arid and 0.20-0.50 semi-arid”.
items.answer: Aridity index

items.stem: Explain how the global atmospheric circulation produces hot deserts.
items.answer: Air rising at the ITCZ flows polewards aloft, cools and sinks at about 30°; sinking air warms adiabatically and its relative humidity falls, so clouds cannot form; the trade winds blowing out of the highs are dry.

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of a hot arid climate.
items.answer: Annual rainfall below 250 mm, falling irregularly in short intense storms; high summer temperatures (over 40 °C maxima); large diurnal range (20 °C or more); low humidity; very high PET.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per characteristic [4]

items.stem: Table 13.1 shows mean annual precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PET) for four stations (mm): Aswan, Egypt: P 1, PET 2 380; In Salah, Algeria: P 16, PET 2 210; Niamey, Niger: P 534, PET 2 000; Jodhpur, India: P 396, PET 1 800. Aridity index = P ÷ PET. Hyper-arid: below 0.05; arid: 0.05-0.20; semi-arid: 0.20-0.50; dry sub-humid: 0.50-0.65. Explain why the aridity index is a better measure of aridity than rainfall alone.
items.answer: It takes account of water lost by evapotranspiration, so a cool place and a hot place with the same rainfall can have very different water availability.

items.stem: Assess the view that the subtropical high pressure belts are the main cause of hot arid climates.
items.answer: For: Most hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian) lie under the descending limbs of the Hadley cells. Against: Cold ocean currents (Atacama, Namib), continentality (interior Australia, Thar margins), rain shadows (Patagonia, parts of the Great Basin) contribute; local factors explain the most extreme deserts. Conclusion: Subtropical highs explain the global pattern, while currents, continentality and relief explain variations and the driest areas.

items.answer: They lie on the margins of the ITCZ or monsoon, so small shifts in its position or ENSO events change whether rain-bearing systems arrive; rainfall comes from a few large storms.

items.stem: Explain how cold ocean currents contribute to aridity.
items.answer: They cool the lowest layer of air, creating a temperature inversion and stable air; little evaporation; onshore air warms over land and its relative humidity falls; fog but little rain.

items.stem: Explain how continentality affects the climate of desert interiors.
items.answer: Distance from the sea means air has lost its moisture; land heats and cools quickly, giving very hot summers, cool winters and large ranges.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a rain shadow.
items.answer: Moist air is forced over mountains, cools adiabatically and loses moisture as rain on the windward side; on the leeward side it descends, warms at the dry adiabatic rate and becomes very dry.

items.answer: Southward shift or weakening of the West African monsoon and ITCZ; changes in Atlantic sea-surface temperatures; aerosols; land degradation reducing moisture recycling; ENSO influences.

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that climate change is the greatest threat to people living on the margins of arid environments.
items.answer: For: Rising temperatures increase evaporation; more variable rainfall and longer droughts reduce yields and pasture; the drylands are expected to expand. Against: Population growth, poverty, conflict (Sahel), overgrazing and poor water management are often more immediate threats; adaptation can reduce risk. Conclusion: Climate change multiplies existing threats, but human pressures and vulnerability determine how serious they become.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the subtropical high pressure belts are the main cause of hot arid climates? In your answer you may refer to Hadley cell and rain shadow.
items.answer: For: Most hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian) lie under the descending limbs of the Hadley cells. Conclusion: Subtropical highs explain the global pattern, while currents, continentality and relief explain variations and the driest areas.

items.stem: Assess the view that climate change is the greatest threat to people living on the margins of arid environments. In your answer you may refer to adaptation, population pressure and land degradation.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how continentality affects the climate of desert interiors. (b) Explain the formation of a rain shadow.
items.answer: (a) Distance from the sea means air has lost its moisture; land heats and cools quickly, giving very hot summers, cool winters and large ranges. (b) Moist air is forced over mountains, cools adiabatically and loses moisture as rain on the windward side; on the leeward side it descends, warms at the dry adiabatic rate and becomes very dry.
